big_idea: Before we count, we can make a smart guess about how many — that is called an estimate.
learning_intention: We are learning to estimate how many objects are in a small group, check our estimate by counting, and continue counting to 20 from any number.
student_learning_goal: I can guess how many pennies are in a jar, then count to check, and I can count to 20 starting from any number.
success_criteria: I can write or say a smart guess about how many pennies are in the jar.
I can count the pennies one at a time and say the total.
I can count on by 1s up to 20 starting from any number my teacher gives me.
lesson_specific_materials: Clear estimation jar with 12–18 pennies (the 'class jar')
Per-pair small jars (paper cups work) each holding 5–15 pennies, varied counts
Coin Path floor cards 0–20 — letter-size cardstock with one big numeral per card, taped to the floor in a line
Anchor chart paper titled 'Our Smart Guess' with two columns: 'I GUESSED' / 'WE COUNTED'
Penny and Nick character illustrations to introduce the unit (cardstock cut-outs)
Quincy the piggy-bank cardstock mascot (propped beside the class jar)

minds_on.hook: Today we welcome Penny, Nick, and their piggy-bank friend Quincy to our classroom. Quincy is FULL of pennies — but he wants to know HOW MANY. Could you make a smart guess?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet with Quincy propped beside the class jar.

'Friends, this is Quincy. He is a piggy bank, and inside this jar is the snack he was saving — pennies. Quincy needs YOUR help. He wants to know HOW MANY — but he is too small to count.'

'Before we count, we make a SMART GUESS — an estimate. Look at the jar — do not shout. Hold up fingers for your guess. If you think 10, hold up TEN fingers. If you think 15, count fifteen. Whisper-tell your guess to your knees.'

Wait while every child guesses. 'Now we count together to check.' Tip the jar onto the carpet; point to each penny; lead the count: 'one, two, three…'.

After the total: 'Some guessed close, some guessed far. Both are okay — that is what an estimate is. Now we know there are exactly ___ pennies.'

Quincy's refrain. Class chants 3x with claps: 'GUESS first — COUNT next! That's how Quincy counts!'
student_actions: Look at Quincy's penny jar without touching it and form a quiet finger-guess.
Whisper-tell their guess to their knees.
Watch the teacher tip the pennies onto the carpet and join the chorus count.
Compare their finger-guess to the real count and notice if they were close, low, or high.

steps.instruction: Whole group: walk the Coin Path. Tape the 0–20 floor cards in a line down the carpet. Invite four volunteers to stand on 0, 1, 2, 3 and have the class chorus-count them. Then place a card-marker on 12 and ask, 'Penny is already at 12. Could we keep counting from there, or do we have to start over at 1?' Take ideas, then model: walk from 12 to 20 stepping on each card and chanting 'thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty'. Repeat with starting numbers 7 and 15. Tell children: 'When we keep going from a number, we are COUNTING ON.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'You can count on from any number. The next number is always one bigger than the one before. Try it with me — I will say the start, you say the next.' Call out 14 and pause; the class chants 15. Call out 8 and pause; the class chants 9. Repeat 4–5 times.

steps.instruction: Send pairs back to their tables. Each pair gets a small jar of pennies (5–15 inside, count varies). Step A: each child writes or draws their estimate on the recording sheet (no peeking inside). Step B: tip the pennies onto the table and count one at a time, lining them up like a row of soldiers. Step C: write the actual count and circle whether the guess was 'close' (within 3) or 'not yet'.
steps.teacher_prompt: Walk pairs through the rule: 'EVERY child estimates first. THEN you count together. NO counting before guessing — that is the secret of estimation.' Remind: 'Line the pennies up so it is easy to count one-by-one. Touch each penny as you say its number.'

steps.instruction: Circulate with the diagnostic checklist. Listen for: (a) whether the child counts each penny exactly once (one-to-one correspondence), (b) whether the child can recite the count sequence beyond 10 without skipping, (c) whether the child can count on when you stop them mid-count and say 'now keep going from 7'. After every pair finishes their first jar, swap jars with the pair beside them and repeat — each child does at least two estimate-and-count rounds.
steps.teacher_prompt: Ask, mid-count: 'Stop right there. You said 6. Without starting over — what comes next?' If the child can answer '7' without restarting, tick the count-on column on your checklist. If they restart at 1, model the count-on once and move on; do not correct repeatedly.

differentiation.for_emerging: Emerging children pair with a stronger partner and use a jar with 5–7 pennies (fewer to track). Their recording sheet is pre-printed with three small dot-circles to show where to draw their guess; they only need to draw the count on the second line.
differentiation.for_extending: Extending children use a jar with 18–20 pennies and a recording sheet that asks for THREE estimates: 'closest to 5, closest to 10, closest to 20'. They circle which one their guess matched. Then they are challenged to count on starting from 14.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Pre-teach 'estimate', 'guess', 'count on' with a hand gesture each child can echo (open palm = guess; finger walking = count on). Provide a number-line strip 0–20 on the table for visual anchoring during the count. Allow drawing dots instead of writing numerals.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER, NO-PURCHASE PATH: skip Coin Path floor cards and recording sheets entirely. Children form a giant whole-class human number line standing in order 1-20. Teacher points at one child as the 'starting number'; everyone from that child onward stomps and chants their number to count on. Estimate by holding up fingers; count by tapping a partner's open palm. Whole lesson runs on bodies + classroom pennies (or any small classroom counters: paper-clips, blocks, beans) — no purchased materials, no printed sheets.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Diagnostic-level evidence on three sub-skills: (1) does the child make any estimate at all, or refuse and demand to count first? (2) does the child preserve one-to-one correspondence when counting up to 15+? (3) does the child count on from a non-1 starting number, or does every count restart at 1?
formative_check.how_to_record: Class diagnostic checklist with one row per child and four columns: 'estimates_before_counting', 'one_to_one_to_15', 'count_on_from_non_1', 'estimate_within_3_of_actual'. Tick as you observe during partner work.

discussion_prompts: When you looked at the jar, what helped you make a smart guess? Did you spot any small groups (a 'lump' of 5 or so) inside?
Penny says she always counts on instead of starting over at 1. Why might that be faster? Show me with your fingers.
consolidation.exit_routine: Refrain chant 3x. Then on the way out the door, each child names ONE penny-jar count they did today AND counts on five more from that number out loud. Example: 'I had 7 pennies — eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve.' Teacher tallies how many children can count on without restarting.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Per-pair recording sheets showing estimate vs actual count for at least two jars per child. Per-child diagnostic checklist with four indicators. Exit-routine count-on tally captured on a single class roster sheet.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: A6.7 estimation and A6.8 count-on are the entry baseline for the unit. Children entering K vary widely — some can already count to 30+ on demand; others restart at 1 every time the teacher pauses. This lesson distinguishes those two profiles before Lesson 2 builds on counting fluency.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child counts every penny twice — or restarts at 1 every time you pause (Gelman & Gallistel, 1978; Sarama & Clements, 2009; Baroody, 2006)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A6.7 estimation and A6.8 count-on, the two most-documented K traps are double-counting (one-to-one correspondence breakdown — touching the same penny while saying two numbers) and reflexive restart (every interruption, even mid-count, sends the child back to 'one').

Gelman & Gallistel's (1978) five counting principles establish that children must master one-to-one (each item gets one and only one count word) AND order-irrelevance (counts can resume from any point) before counting becomes a reliable measurement tool. Restart-at-1 is precisely the order-irrelevance failure: the child treats the count word sequence as a recitation poem that only starts at 'one', not as a label-pairing they can resume. Baroody (2006) traces estimation development and notes that K children initially treat estimates as 'wrong guesses' and resist them — a self-protective stance that disappears only when teachers explicitly decouple estimation accuracy from being right.

Sarama & Clements (2009) place count-on (A6.8) at the level immediately above stable-order rote counting in their counting trajectory — it's the first cognitive move that lets children use counting as a TOOL rather than a song. A K child who can't count on cannot do part-part-whole addition in L2 ('I have 7, three more is…') without finger-laborious recount, so this lesson's diagnostic determines whether L2 will land for each child.

Why this matters: both traps are visible during Step 2 partner work and both are highly remediable when caught at K — left unaddressed, they bottleneck Grade 1 addition.

This walkthrough covers what to say when you spot each, and how to capture the diagnostic without correcting the child into the right answer.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Each pair has a paper cup of pennies and a recording sheet. The teacher carries a clipboard with the class diagnostic roster. The Coin Path strip should still be taped to the floor — children who restart at 1 can be redirected there to physically walk through count-on once before returning to their jar.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Walk to a pair mid-count. The child has 8 pennies on the table and is touching one penny twice (saying 'six, seven' on the same coin). Crouch to their level. 'Wait one second — show me which penny you just counted as seven.' The child points. 'Show me six.' If they point to the SAME penny, gently slide it slightly aside. 'When we count, each penny only gets ONE number. Let us start that row again — touch and slide.' Model touching the first penny, sliding it half an inch to the right, saying 'one'. Watch them do the next two; affirm or remodel. Note 'one_to_one_under_15' on the checklist — tick if they self-correct, leave blank if they continue double-counting.

For the restart-at-1 child: ask 'how many do you have so far?' Listen — they say '6'. 'Great. Now without starting over, count on from 6 — what is the next penny?' If they freeze, walk them to the Coin Path strip. 'Stand on 6. Now step forward.' Have them say 'seven' as they step on 7. 'Step forward.' They say 'eight'. Walk from 6 to 12. 'See? You did not start at 1 — you kept going from 6. That is COUNTING ON.' Send them back to the jar with the prompt 'try counting on this time — I will be back to listen.' Tick 'count_on_from_non_1' only if they do it independently on the second attempt.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Counts the same penny multiple times; total is far higher than the actual count. Has not yet built one-to-one correspondence.
(Mid) Counts each penny once but restarts at 1 every time the teacher asks a follow-up. Knows the count sequence; does not yet know it is reusable mid-count.
(Strong) Self-corrects double-counts (slides the penny aside) and counts on from a non-1 start without prompting.
(Stretched) Counts on through a teen number (14, 15, 16, 17) without slowing or restarting, and offers an estimation strategy ('I saw two groups of 5 so I guessed 10').
common_misconceptions: Each touch of my finger is a count, even on the same penny. (Tip: physically separate the pennies — slide aside on count.)
Counting always starts at 1. Any pause means starting over. (Tip: use the Coin Path strip to make the resumption point physical.)
Estimation = the right answer. Children think their guess must match the count and feel bad if it is off by 5. (Tip: celebrate every guess that uses a strategy, not just the close ones.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child double-counts (touches same penny twice, breaks one-to-one): slide-and-count drill. Physically separate counted pennies from un-counted ones; each counted penny moves half-an-inch right; the visual gap rebuilds Gelman & Gallistel's one-to-one principle in seconds. Repeat for the next 3 jars; tick 'one_to_one_to_15' only when self-correcting.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child restarts at 1 every interruption (order-irrelevance failure): walk the Coin Path floor strip from a non-1 start. 'Stand on 6. Step forward — say 7. Step forward — say 8.' Embodied count-on: restating 'count on' verbally rarely works at K, but walking it does. Re-teach by foot before re-teaching by voice. Tick 'count_on_from_non_1' only on independent second attempt.

DIAGNOSTIC C — child refuses to estimate (treats it as a wrong guess and demands to count first): reframe explicitly with Baroody's (2006) framing. 'Was your guess HIGH or LOW? Either way that is GREAT information for next time.' Decouple estimation accuracy from being right. Stay until the child offers a guess; celebrate the strategy ('you saw a group of 5'), not the closeness.

worksheet_brief.purpose: End-of-lesson consolidation. Children record an estimate-then-count for one or two pictured jars and then practise count-on from a teen number. Captures diagnostic-level evidence for A6.7 (was an estimate made, was it within 3?) and A6.8 (can the child write the next 5 numbers from a given start?).

parts_outline.task: Look at Quincy's first penny jar. Write or draw your smart guess. Then count the pennies and write the actual number.
Look at Quincy's second penny jar. Write your guess, then write the actual count. Circle: was your guess close, low, or high?
Penny is at the number 14. Write the next FIVE numbers as she counts on along the Coin Path.
